name: Rosa Okafor

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. We don't sell or campaign for anything. Your answers are confidential. What is an ordinary workday like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I carry boards from the lock-up, set out the fixings and help the carpenter put up partitions on the Canal Road housing site. I'm fifty-eight and still junior because I switched into site work after years running a laundry; I left school before the final exams. I earn well for the grade, partly because this builder pays a fair site rate, but I'm still learning to judge timber by eye. My partner Ellis cooks at the hospital, and our two children are grown. I like leaving a clean, square room behind, though the dust gets into everything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew a little computer help with deliveries is fine if it doesn't become an excuse to skip a person on the shift. The partition still needs our hands and a proper safety check.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my pay is safe on Canal Road, and Ellis has a steady hospital kitchen post. We have more than eight months of expenses saved and several builders nearby, so a small software change doesn't put our home in danger.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll carry on setting partitions and ask the site steward whether any ordering change affects shifts. In the first year I'd keep our ordinary savings transfer and take the same paid workdays; I won't start using a chatbot to decide how to fix a wall.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm enough about this picture. The dust and the rush to finish rooms are more immediate than any app.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why ask the steward if you think the work is safe?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I want someone watching the rota before a small cut becomes normal. That is part of looking after the whole crew, even when my own rent is covered.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What did the laundry teach you about new systems?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A booking system once made tidy lists while leaving my staff to sort real lost shirts. A neat screen can hide extra work for people on their feet.

say: I'd accept **delivery software** if shift staffing and safety remain sound.
I'd remind the crew a **partition** still needs hands and inspection.
think: My Canal Road pay and Ellis's **hospital wage** feel secure.
Our **eight-month reserve** and nearby builders give us room if a small change occurs.
do: Keep setting **partitions** and taking the same paid site days on Canal Road.
Ask the **site steward** whether ordering changes affect shifts.
feel: **Calm** about limited software, with dust and rushed work more immediate.
S0.quote: A neat screen can hide extra work for people on their feet.
fieldNote: Rosa's confidence comes from **higher site pay**, Ellis's hospital wage and a reserve exceeding eight months.
She consults the steward for crew-wide staffing, reflecting a **prior booking system** that shifted hidden work onto employees.

steps.text: Keep setting partitions on the Canal Road site
Ask the site steward about staffing after ordering changes

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ordering and planning software may save time, but workers should see the new targets before managers quietly drop posts. I would ask our site union branch to bring the office and site staff into the same meeting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The hands-on work looks fairly solid for now, although fewer people doing estimates could mean fewer jobs reaching our crew. I have savings and other local builders, but I don't want the slower junior workers to be treated as spare parts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll attend the next union branch meeting and ask for a written account of which office and site roles are changing. In the first year I'd keep the Canal Road shifts and check the vacancy boards at nearby builders if the next contract starts slipping; I would not switch employers on a rumour.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy for the crew, especially the younger people paying high rent. My own wage looks likely to continue, but the planning side could change what comes down to the site.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What exactly would you want in writing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want the number of posts, the dates and who checks safety after a software order changes. A general promise to consult means very little without a rota we can compare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you speak to a younger worker about the change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell a young labourer to keep copies of hours and to come to the branch meeting with questions. They shouldn't have to guess alone why the office stopped booking work.

say: I'd ask managers to show **new targets** before posts disappear.
I'd bring **office and site staff** into a union meeting.
think: Fewer estimators might mean **fewer site contracts**, though my own wage looks fairly safe.
I worry junior workers without my **savings cushion** would take the first hit.
do: Attend the **union meeting** and request written staffing numbers.
Keep **Canal Road shifts** while the contract continues.
Check nearby **vacancies** if the next contract slips.
feel: **Uneasy for colleagues**, while my own earnings look likely to continue.
S1.quote: A general promise to consult means very little without a rota we can compare.
fieldNote: Rosa focuses on **staffing records** and safety responsibility, not on learning the ordering software herself.
Her own **financial buffer** tempers income fear, while she takes specific union action for exposed colleagues.

steps.text: Attend the union branch meeting and request staffing figures
Keep taking Canal Road site shifts
Check nearby builders if the next contract slips

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say full thinking AI by 2028 could empty the office before a robot touches a wall, and we need a worker seat at every staffing decision. By 2031, when robots can do site work, safety rules and fair notice must be in writing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll be sixty when office estimates can vanish and sixty-three when the robot could set partitions. Our savings buy time, but if the firm cuts site hours sharply, Ellis's wage alone may not cover everything we planned for retirement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting now I'll ask the union branch to negotiate notice and paid placement with nearby builders, and I'll keep taking my shifts. In 2029 I'll stay on paid partition work if the site needs me, but I'll apply to other local site crews if the rota falls below four days a week; I won't pay for a course chosen by the employer without a clear job at the end.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel angry about the speed, and anxious about losing a large part of my wage at sixty-three. I have places to apply and money for a short gap, so I can make decisions before the bills turn urgent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why four days a week as your line?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Four days lets us keep saving a little while Ellis pays the regular food bill. Below that, we would be living off the reserve before we had agreed how to use it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want the union agreement to cover?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I want advance notice, proper safety checks around robots and a paid route into remaining site jobs. Workers should not have to sign away safety to keep the last shift.

say: I'd demand **worker seats** before office and site staffing decisions.
I'd insist on **written safety rules** before 2031 site robots arrive.
think: At **sixty**, office work may disappear before my partition shifts do.
At **sixty-three**, a sharp site cut could threaten our retirement savings despite the reserve.
do: Ask the **union branch** to negotiate notice, safety and paid placement.
Keep **paid partitions** in 2029 if work remains.
Apply to **local site crews** if the rota drops below four days.
feel: **Angry and anxious** about possible wage loss, with practical options still available.
S2.quote: Workers should not have to sign away safety to keep the last shift.
fieldNote: Rosa's income concern begins with the **2031 hands-on robot date**, while she tracks the earlier risk to office staff.
Her **four-day threshold** links a possible job search to actual household cash rather than a general fear of technology.

steps.text: Ask the union branch to negotiate robot safety and notice
Keep taking paid partition shifts in 2029
Apply to local site crews if shifts fall below four days

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the branch that five years is enough to bargain with evidence instead of accepting a last-minute memo. We should get the staffing figures each year and make the builder show how robot work will be checked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll be sixty-three when thinking AI arrives and sixty-six when the robots can handle partitions. Ellis and I could possibly stop my site work by then, but we need the real numbers; higher pay today does not itself buy retirement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep working, ask the branch to collect yearly staffing and safety figures, and save the difference from my better paid months. In 2032 I'd take paid site shifts while available and sit with Ellis to compare our savings with expected bills; if I still need wages as robots spread, I'd apply to a nearby builder before dropping these shifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel more in command with the extra years, though I don't trust promises made without figures. A slower change gives us time to protect our choices rather than rush into a bad job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you decide if you could stop working?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ellis and I would put the actual savings, wages and future bills on one page and see what is missing. I won't tell our grown children we are retiring until that page adds up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you learn to operate the robots?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would watch a properly supervised trial, but I am not volunteering to train on a machine with unclear safety rules. If a paid role is real and safe, I would consider it then.

say: I'd seek **yearly staffing figures** and evidence before bargaining.
I'd require **robot safety checks** to be shown, not promised.
think: At **sixty-six**, I may be able to stop site work, but only after checking the figures.
Today's **higher pay** does not prove retirement will be affordable.
do: Keep **paid work** and save more from better paid months.
Collect **staffing and safety figures** through the union.
Compare **household bills** in 2032 and apply elsewhere if wages are still needed.
feel: More **in command**, though unsupported promises still trouble me.
S3.quote: I won't tell our grown children we are retiring until that page adds up.
fieldNote: Rosa treats a **possible retirement** at sixty-six as a calculation to complete with Ellis, not a guaranteed outcome.
Her union plan becomes an **annual evidence request**, and she remains unwilling to train on an unsafe machine.

steps.text: Save more from better paid site months
Ask the union branch for annual staffing and safety figures
Keep taking paid site shifts in 2032
Apply to a nearby builder if wages remain necessary

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade gives workers a chance to put safety and fair notice into the rules while they still have jobs. I won't call a 2039 robot safe just because it comes later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll be sixty-eight when thinking AI comes and seventy-one when site robots arrive. Ellis and I may have finished paid work by then, but I won't assume it; I want the freedom to choose, backed by savings and a fair site record.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep taking well-paid partition shifts now and add to our reserve from each full month. In 2037, if I still need income, I'll take paid site work and ask the union branch what safety rules cover AI-written orders; before 2039, Ellis and I will review whether I can stop climbing scaffolds and live on the income we actually have.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel fairly calm about the distant technology, though I'm not comfortable with someone else deciding workers' last day. My knees and site safety still matter while I earn these next ten years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if your grown children offered to help later?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd thank them, but they have their own bills. My grown children's visits are company, not a line in our retirement sums.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you move to follow site work at seventy-one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, not on the chance of another job; there are plenty of builders near our home already. I would first check whether a safe paid local role exists and whether we need it.

say: I'd press for **safety and notice** rules during the decade.
I'd refuse to call a **2039 robot** safe merely because it arrives later.
think: At **sixty-eight**, I may still want paid work after thinking AI arrives.
At **seventy-one**, retirement depends on actual savings and Ellis's income.
do: Keep **partition shifts** and build the reserve from full months.
Take **paid site work** in 2037 if our income requires it.
Ask the **union branch** about AI-written order safety and check retirement figures.
feel: Fairly **calm** about distant dates, while current site safety matters.
S4.quote: My grown children's visits are company, not a line in our retirement sums.
fieldNote: Ten years and **strong resources** make Rosa relatively calm, while she keeps safety and income decisions open.
She does not count **grown children** as support or plan a speculative move despite many local builders.

steps.text: Keep taking paid partition shifts while fit
Add to savings after full paid months
Ask the union branch about AI order safety before 2039

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The fast 2028 picture worries me most because the robot date lands when I might still need my site wage. Proper advance notice, an enforceable safety agreement and paid openings at nearby builders would help us choose before a sudden cut.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask who pays when a robot's mistake leaves a worker injured or a wall unsafe. That has to be settled while workers still have a voice, not after the first accident.

headlineQuote: You didn't ask who pays when a robot's mistake leaves a worker injured or a wall unsafe.
portrait: Rosa is a **fifty-eight-year-old junior** site worker who entered carpentry after running a laundry.
Her **higher site pay**, Ellis's hospital wage and more than eight months saved provide a strong cushion.
She avoids AI tools and uses the **union branch** to seek staffing records and safety rules.
She will keep **paid site work** until household figures support a retirement decision.
biggestWorry: The **2028 path** could cut her site wage around the 2031 robot arrival, before retirement is settled.
whatWouldHelp: She wants **advance notice**, enforceable robot safety rules and paid local site openings.
